data.question_intent: Inquire about specific businesses targeted by structural cost actions and the profitability dynamics of Best Egg.
data.question_quote: A couple of areas where I was getting some questions on the results. So, I think one you've already touched on a bit, so with regards to the structural cost actions, but thinking about it in a bit more detail. I guess [I'm] trying to understand, is there any specific businesses beyond just the broader spread across the business units, that that's the incremental £300 million is targeted at, and any real examples of how that money is being spent. That should be helpful. And then secondly, just with regards to Best Egg and the profitability that it seemed to report for the last couple of months. It seems to take a bit of a step down, I know there's commentary about the spread pressure related to the funding costs versus the APRs, but it seems to swing from actually something which was profitable when you purchased it, to something that you is essentially loss making the last couple months. So quite volatile there. So just trying to understand the dynamics and how we should think about the profitability of that business and [how it develops] over the coming months, notwithstanding the cost reductions [that you've called out].
data.answer_quote: Okay, so let me start with SCAs. So, I wouldn't call out any specific businesses. You're going to see it across the entirety of the firm - front office, middle office, back office impacting. It relates organisational simplification. So, I'm not going to call out specific examples now, but we will give you much more detail at Q3 and Q4, when we're actually spending that money. But think about all simplifications, think about process simplification and then the reduction in costs associated with that. In relation to Best Egg, I think the confusion here actually relates, not to Best Egg, but to American Airlines. So, when American Airlines left the platform, I think everybody has accounted for the NII associated with the balances, but remember that American Airlines was in large part a transactor book, that's why it was low margin. So you're also seeing when American Airlines leaves the platform, non-NII falls. So then what you've got is non-NII falling from two months worth of loss from American Airlines, then replaced by non-NII coming in from Best Egg. So if you are assuming that actually, there was no loss of non-NII, then what you're doing is you're seeing a suppress number for Best Egg. So, I think that's where the confusion is coming from. So, what you're seeing is non-NII pickup, there is a very small NII impact, very small from retained balances. [Best Egg] costs coming in at $45 million per month. But I mean this business is the opposite of volatile, that's what it's designed to be. It's designed to be a largely fee driven servicing model. So you're going to see a high cost to income ratio but a low level of capital against it. I'm really hopeful that when we come to Q3, that will give you a much cleaner read and again we will sort of talk you through that one again.
